Many of the people who need help most receive the least.

The welfare of the poor, the sick, and the marginalized depends on better-off strangers, whose attention, concern, and resources are captured almost entirely by their own families, friends, and communities (Balliet et al., 2014; Brewer, 1999; Jones & Rachlin, 2006).
text.formatted: The welfare of the poor, the sick, and the marginalized depends on better-off strangers, whose attention, concern, and resources are captured almost entirely by their own families, friends, and communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Balliet et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Brewer, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Jones & Rachlin, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: One reason is social categorization: people readily perceive those in greatest need as outgroup members, and the needs of outgroups, such as immigrants and transgender people, attract less attention and receive less weight in their decisions than comparable ingroup needs (Cikara et al., 2011; Levine et al., 2005; Nguyen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One reason is social categorization: people readily perceive those in greatest need as outgroup members, and the needs of outgroups, such as immigrants and transgender people, attract less attention and receive less weight in their decisions than comparable ingroup needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Cikara et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Levine et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Nguyen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This parochial altruism (Bernhard et al., 2006; Choi & Bowles, 2007) skews the allocation of human generosity: most help makes already highly privileged people slightly better off while even the most basic needs of millions of people go almost completely unmet (Caviola et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This parochial altruism <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Bernhard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Choi & Bowles, 2007)</ref> skews the allocation of human generosity: most help makes already highly privileged people slightly better off while even the most basic needs of millions of people go almost completely unmet <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Caviola et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The same ingroup-outgroup psychology that biases whom people help also breeds prejudice against outgroup members (Devine, 1989) and, at its worst, open intergroup hostility.
text.formatted: The same ingroup-outgroup psychology that biases whom people help also breeds prejudice against outgroup members <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Devine, 1989</ref>) and, at its worst, open intergroup hostility.

text.text: Classic research on intergroup conflict found that people's behavior toward an outgroup can be durably improved by cooperative intergroup contact (Allport, 1954; Mousa, 2020; Sherif, 1966; Woodley et al., 2025), and by perspective taking (e.g., Batson, 1997; Cialdini et al., 1997; Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000; Neuberg et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Classic research on intergroup conflict found that people's behavior toward an outgroup can be durably improved by cooperative intergroup contact <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allport, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Mousa, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Sherif, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Woodley et al., 2025)</ref>, and by perspective taking (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Batson, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Cialdini et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Neuberg et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Both are assumed to work by improving attitudes toward the outgroup (e.g., reducing prejudice and dehumanization) and increasing perceived similarity, connectedness, and interpersonal warmth (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2008; Todd & Galinsky, 2014).
text.formatted: Both are assumed to work by improving attitudes toward the outgroup (e.g., reducing prejudice and dehumanization) and increasing perceived similarity, connectedness, and interpersonal warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Pettigrew & Tropp, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Todd & Galinsky, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, training people to cultivate compassion can increase costly helping toward suffering strangers (Weng et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Similarly, training people to cultivate compassion can increase costly helping toward suffering strangers <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Weng et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, rigorous field experiments suggest that the effects of such prejudice-reduction interventions are limited in size, scope, and duration (Mousa, 2020; Paluck et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, rigorous field experiments suggest that the effects of such prejudice-reduction interventions are limited in size, scope, and duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Mousa, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Paluck et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, inducing empathy for one outgroup can cause preferential treatment of that outgroup at the expense of other outgroups and the greater good (Batson, Batson, et al., 1995; Batson, Klein, et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Moreover, inducing empathy for one outgroup can cause preferential treatment of that outgroup at the expense of other outgroups and the greater good <ref type="bibr">(Batson, Batson, et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batson, Klein, et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we investigate a complementary mechanism: learning to make social decisions more considerately.

Unlike interventions that target people's feelings about a particular group, this approach can transfer across situations and outgroups, without the favoritism empathy induction can produce (Batson, Batson, et al., 1995; Batson, Klein, et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Unlike interventions that target people's feelings about a particular group, this approach can transfer across situations and outgroups, without the favoritism empathy induction can produce <ref type="bibr">(Batson, Batson, et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batson, Klein, et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work suggests that learning to decide more considerately may be partly driven by strategy selection learning (Maier et al., 2026): learning when to use which cognitive strategy by trying out candidate strategies and learning from how the resulting decisions turn out (Lieder & Griffiths, 2017).
text.formatted: Recent work suggests that learning to decide more considerately may be partly driven by strategy selection learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Maier et al., 2026)</ref>: learning when to use which cognitive strategy by trying out candidate strategies and learning from how the resulting decisions turn out <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Lieder & Griffiths, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In this article, we apply this idea to social dilemmas, situations that pit the interests of the individual or their ingroup against the interests of (distant) others (Dawes, 1980; Van Lange et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In this article, we apply this idea to social dilemmas, situations that pit the interests of the individual or their ingroup against the interests of (distant) others <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Dawes, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Van Lange et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with the idea that strategy selection learning shapes how people make social decisions, Rand et al. (2014) argued that when people forego their own self-interest in a social dilemma to benefit others, it is because they rely on social heuristics they learned in social environments where cooperating with others pays off (Peysakhovich & Rand, 2016).
text.formatted: Consistent with the idea that strategy selection learning shapes how people make social decisions, <ref type="bibr">Rand et al. (2014)</ref> argued that when people forego their own self-interest in a social dilemma to benefit others, it is because they rely on social heuristics they learned in social environments where cooperating with others pays off <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Peysakhovich & Rand, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Maier et al. (2026) found that when people repeatedly make decisions that affect others, they learn to select the strategies that have been most beneficial to the greater good in their experience.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Maier et al. (2026)</ref> found that when people repeatedly make decisions that affect others, they learn to select the strategies that have been most beneficial to the greater good in their experience.

text.text: They call this mechanism metacognitive moral learning because it produces lasting, experience-driven changes in how people regulate their moral decision-making process (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: They call this mechanism metacognitive moral learning because it produces lasting, experience-driven changes in how people regulate their moral decision-making process (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This includes learning when to override moral rules (e.g., "Do no harm") by utilitarian reasoning.

Their computational model formalizes this as reinforcement learning over decision mechanisms: judging that a previous decision was morally right reinforces the mechanism that produced it, whereas judging it morally wrong makes that mechanism less likely to be used again.
Critically, those judgments are informed by the decision's consequences.

Supporting this account, Maier et al. (2026) found that participants learned to follow moral rules or to override them with cost-benefit reasoning depending on which strategy produced better outcomes in the scenarios they encountered.
text.formatted: Supporting this account, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Maier et al. (2026)</ref> found that participants learned to follow moral rules or to override them with cost-benefit reasoning depending on which strategy produced better outcomes in the scenarios they encountered.

text.text: Beyond shaping which decision strategy people select, learning from the consequences of past decisions can also adjust a second, distinct target: how much weight people assign to each stakeholder's welfare when they decide (moral weight learning; Spiteri, Maier, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Beyond shaping which decision strategy people select, learning from the consequences of past decisions can also adjust a second, distinct target: how much weight people assign to each stakeholder's welfare when they decide (moral weight learning; <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Spiteri, Maier, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Through this mechanism, realizing that you harmed distant others because you did not give them enough consideration can lead you to up-weight their welfare in subsequent decisions.
This mechanism operates on the decision weights that strategies like cost-benefit reasoning draw on.
Although these theorized mechanisms could make people more prosocial toward outgroups (outgroup prosociality), this hypothesis has not yet been tested empirically.
Moral learning in social dilemmas is difficult by default.
People learn significantly less from their decisions' consequences for others than from the consequences for themselves (Rhoads et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People learn significantly less from their decisions' consequences for others than from the consequences for themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Rhoads et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, a single social dilemma decision has direct and indirect, as well as immediate and long-term effects on many different stakeholders.
Decision-makers reliably encounter the immediate consequences for themselves and for people close to them, but they rarely experience the delayed consequences for distant others.
For instance, people splitting their savings between gifts for their children and donations for global development will experience most of the benefits of the former but (almost) none of the latter.
This can bias their evaluation of whether they made the right choice and their takeaways for future decisions.
People's limited attention further exacerbates this bias (Spiteri, Gao, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: People's limited attention further exacerbates this bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Spiteri, Gao, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this article, we develop and test Systematic Moral Reflection (SMR), a novel intervention designed to promote moral weight learning alongside strategy selection learning: it teaches people to adopt more deliberate decision strategies and to place greater weight on the welfare of distant others.
Figure 1 depicts this learning loop and where SMR intervenes.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> depicts this learning loop and where SMR intervenes.

text.text: A decision strategy produces a decision, the decision produces consequences, and the decisionmaker observes some of those consequences, attends to and processes a subset of them, and evaluates the decision in their light.
The resulting evaluation reinforces or weakens whatever the learner holds in mind as the cause of the outcome.
By default, that is the action itself.
Thus, a decision-maker who never reflects on how they decided will rarely learn better decision strategies because learning cannot reinforce a cause that is not mentally represented.
SMR intervenes at two points where this process can fall short.

At the evaluation stage, it directs attention to the people the decision affected most, asks the decision-maker to take their perspective and consider how they would judge the decision, and asks whether a better decision was available.
This helps people learn from how their decision affected distant others.
At the learning stage, it directs people to derive a general lesson about their decision process.
This requires deliberate effort that people rarely make unprompted.
The Socratic questions for this stage ask how the decision was made, whether a better strategy was available, and how to decide differently in the future.
This helps people learn useful general lessons about how to make better decisions.
In this way, SMR improves the learning signal and channels it into deeper, more generalizable change.

The obstacles described above are analogous to the difficulty of learning from delayed consequences, which prevents people from discovering far-sighted decision strategies. Becker et al. (2023) found that people can overcome these challenges by reflecting systematically: they were significantly more likely to discover far-sighted strategies when Socratic questions directed their attention to how far ahead they had planned and how well their decisions turned out.
text.formatted: The obstacles described above are analogous to the difficulty of learning from delayed consequences, which prevents people from discovering far-sighted decision strategies. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Becker et al. (2023)</ref> found that people can overcome these challenges by reflecting systematically: they were significantly more likely to discover far-sighted strategies when Socratic questions directed their attention to how far ahead they had planned and how well their decisions turned out.

text.text: Systematic reflection also boosts learning from experience in many other domains (Ellis et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Systematic reflection also boosts learning from experience in many other domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Ellis et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: SMR is the first intervention to adapt this evidence-based approach to prosocial decisionmaking, asking people Socratic questions about their previous social decisions (see Table 2).
text.formatted: SMR is the first intervention to adapt this evidence-based approach to prosocial decisionmaking, asking people Socratic questions about their previous social decisions (see Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Its Socratic questioning connects SMR to the Kohlbergian tradition of fostering moral learning through the discussion of moral dilemmas (Blatt & Kohlberg, 1975; Kohlberg & Hersh, 1977), but it directs that questioning at the consequences of a decision the person actually made, and at how they made it rather than at how they justify it.
text.formatted: Its Socratic questioning connects SMR to the Kohlbergian tradition of fostering moral learning through the discussion of moral dilemmas <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Blatt & Kohlberg, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kohlberg & Hersh, 1977)</ref>, but it directs that questioning at the consequences of a decision the person actually made, and at how they made it rather than at how they justify it.

text.text: This article tests whether properly facilitated metacognitive moral learning can increase outgroup prosociality.
We test seven predictions of this account in five preregistered experiments (see Table 5).
text.formatted: We test seven predictions of this account in five preregistered experiments (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">5</ref>).

text.text: Our theory's first and most fundamental prediction is that guiding people to systematically reflect on a past intergroup decision makes their subsequent behavior toward outgroups more prosocial.
All five experiments test this prediction, using consequential decisions.
Because SMR incorporates perspective taking and evokes empathy for outgroup members, alternative accounts also predict such an effect.
The remaining six predictions are distinctive: they follow from the claim that SMR changes how people decide, and attitudechange accounts either do not make them or predict otherwise.
The second prediction follows from what drives metacognitive moral learning.

Because the loop in Figure 1 is driven by the decision-maker's evaluation of their own past decision, the more negatively participants evaluate their first decision, the more their subsequent intergroup behavior should change.
text.formatted: Because the loop in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> is driven by the decision-maker's evaluation of their own past decision, the more negatively participants evaluate their first decision, the more their subsequent intergroup behavior should change.

text.text: Accounts on which reflection primes prosocial norms make no such prediction.
The third prediction is that SMR will change the decision process people use to make choices in intergroup dilemmas.

Concretely, we predict that SMR will teach people to make intergroup decisions more deliberately, pay more attention to how their choices might affect distant others, and give those consequences more weight in future decisions.
Moreover, the lessons participants formulate should predict subsequent changes in their behavior toward outgroups.
We test this prediction by analyzing participants' written lessons and their considerations in subsequent intergroup decisions.
The fourth prediction concerns the mediators of SMR's effects on outgroup prosociality.

If SMR works by teaching people to decide differently, then the resulting changes in their decision process, including what consequences they attend to and how much weight they place on the outgroup's welfare, should partially mediate the effect of SMR on outgroup prosociality.

Moreover, because SMR teaches general strategies for social decision-making, rather than group-specific attitudes, its effects should not be reducible to the mechanisms of perspectivetaking and empathy-induction interventions, such as increased oneness with the outgroup (Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000) or changes in people's beliefs and feelings about the outgroup.
text.formatted: Moreover, because SMR teaches general strategies for social decision-making, rather than group-specific attitudes, its effects should not be reducible to the mechanisms of perspectivetaking and empathy-induction interventions, such as increased oneness with the outgroup <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000)</ref> or changes in people's beliefs and feelings about the outgroup.

text.text: Experiment 3 tests these predictions, using real donations.
The fifth prediction is transfer across multiple outgroups and behaviors.

Because moral learning updates decision procedures and the weight attached to distant others in general rather than attitudes toward a particular group, its benefits should extend to groups the intervention never mentioned.
Experiments 2 and 3 test this prediction, and Experiment S2 probes its boundary.
The sixth prediction concerns SMR's relationship to its ingredients.

Because metacognitive moral learning adds guided deliberation about one's own past decision, and the derivation of an explicit lesson from it, to perspective taking and empathy induction, SMR should increase helping behavior toward the outgroup more than either of those interventions alone.
Experiment 3 tests this prediction by comparing SMR against both.
The seventh prediction is that, because the effects of SMR reflect learning rather than transient emotional states, the increase in helping behavior should persist for at least a week.
Experiment 3 tests this prediction as well.

Throughout this article, we examine the effects of SMR on a past social-dilemma decision, in which participants, in the role of a protagonist, had to weigh a small benefit for themselves and their ingroup against a large benefit for a distant outgroup in greater need.
We predicted that SMR would teach people to prioritize the outgroup's needs more strongly in analogous future decisions.
Experiment 1 provides the first and most direct test of this hypothesis.
After seeing the outcomes of their first decision, half of the participants were guided to systematically reflect on it, and then all of them made a second, comparable decision.
Experiment 1 served as a proof of concept in a volunteering dilemma, which weighed the needs of an impoverished outgroup against a person's own time and their family.

A preregistered replication and extension of this experiment in a donation dilemma (Experiment S1) is summarized at the end of this section and reported in full in Section S3 of the Supplemental Materials.

text.text: We recruited English-speaking adults located in the United States via Prolific.

We posted the experimental (SMR) and control conditions as two mutually exclusive Prolific HITs with the same name and description; once a participant accepted either HIT, they were redirected to the corresponding Qualtrics survey and became ineligible for the other.
As preregistered, we continued data collection until 255 participants had completed each condition.

We chose this sample size to achieve 80% power to detect a small effect on the second decision, after accounting for attention-check exclusions and the reduced efficiency of the nonparametric ANCOVA used as the primary analysis.

The retained sample of 435 participants, together with the observed correlation of r = .49 between the first and second decisions, provides 80% power to detect an effect of d = 0.21 in a one-tailed test at α = .05.
Each group received a bonus that increased its median wage to $9.50 per hour.
We excluded participants who failed any preregistered attention checks before analysis; retention was comparable across conditions.
Table 1 summarizes sample sizes, demographics, and compensation.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarizes sample sizes, demographics, and compensation.

text.text: This experiment used a between-subjects design with two conditions: SMR and control.
Both conditions completed the same two social dilemma decisions (described below); the SMR condition additionally completed a systematic moral reflection exercise between the two decisions.
The second decision served as the primary, preregistered measure of outgroup prosociality.

The experiment presented two social dilemmas embedded in a single cover story, in which the participant took the role of a protagonist who repeatedly faced a conflict between the welfare of a distant, impoverished outgroup and the interests of an ingroup and themselves.
The two dilemmas were matched in structure but differed in surface details so that the second decision was clearly distinct from the first.
After the first decision, all participants were shown the outcome of their decision for both groups.
Participants took the role of one of two full-time employees of a food-assistance nonprofit serving people in need in the local community.

In each dilemma, the protagonist could allocate their free time between volunteering unpaid hours to help the short-staffed organization meet its target of feeding people in need and being with their family (Decision 1) or earning money for a future family vacation (Decision 2).
Participants indicated how many hours they would volunteer on a slider ranging from 0 to 20 hours in 1-hour increments.
Each social dilemma was illustrated with images generated with DALL-E 3 (OpenAI, 2023) from prompts describing the scenario depicted in the corresponding vignette.
The scenarios and response scales are described below; the full vignettes are reproduced in Section S5.1 of the Supplemental Materials.
The systematic moral reflection intervention was implemented as a series of Socratic questions within the experiment's Qualtrics survey.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the Socratic questions guided participants to evaluate the first decision from the perspectives of everyone who was affected by it (Steps 1-5), analyze how they reached that decision (Step 6), identify how this decision process could be improved (Steps 7-8), and plan to apply those improvements to future decisions (Step 9).
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, the Socratic questions guided participants to evaluate the first decision from the perspectives of everyone who was affected by it (Steps 1-5), analyze how they reached that decision (Step 6), identify how this decision process could be improved (Steps 7-8), and plan to apply those improvements to future decisions (Step 9).

The full text of every question is available in the experiment's Qualtrics survey in the project's online repository.

Participants describe how they reached their decision by answering three questions about i) how long they thought about the decision, ii) how much of that time they had spent on thinking about consequences for themselves, and iii) how much of that time they had spent on thinking about consequences for others.
Participants then rate how important considerations about consequences for i) themselves, ii) people they know, and iii) people they don't know personally were for their decision.

After that, they rate how much they had relied on each of the ten decision strategies listed in Table A1 in Appendix A. Those decision strategies range from non-moral strategies, such as "I have chosen this action many times before" and "I followed my gut feeling", to "I followed the norms, rules, or expectations of my community," and explicitly moral strategies, such as "I followed my moral intuitions about right and wrong", "I wanted to ensure fairness", and "I wanted to maximize the sum of everyone's wellbeing."
text.formatted: After that, they rate how much they had relied on each of the ten decision strategies listed in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref> in Appendix A. Those decision strategies range from non-moral strategies, such as "I have chosen this action many times before" and "I followed my gut feeling", to "I followed the norms, rules, or expectations of my community," and explicitly moral strategies, such as "I followed my moral intuitions about right and wrong", "I wanted to ensure fairness", and "I wanted to maximize the sum of everyone's wellbeing."

text.text: 2 Evaluating the most important consequences
Participants systematically reflect on the outcomes of their decision.

They are reminded of the outcome of their decision and then on who was most positively/negatively affected by their decision, put themselves into those people's shoes as they experienced the consequences, and then rate how bad it was for one person to experience those consequences and how bad it was for all affected individuals to experience those consequences.

Participants first complete this process for the group or individual who was most positively affected by their decision, and then complete it for the group or individual who was most negatively affected by their decision.
To help participants overcome omission bias, we ask them to consider the effect of having chosen what they chose over the alternative that would have been worst/best for others.
3 Taking an outside perspective.

Participants judge how good and how selfish they were from the perspectives of the people who were most positively affected and from the perspective of the people who were most negatively affected by their decision.
4 Attending to (moral) emotions Participants report how good or how bad they felt about their decision.
Participants evaluate the quality of their decision from a moral perspective.
6 Auditing the decision process for potential mistakes
Participants critically examine the process through which they reached the decision with an eye to how it could be improved.

The questions specifically direct their attention to whether they had given the decision enough thought and whether they had paid enough attention to the decision's potential consequences for all stakeholders.
Participants then rate their overall satisfaction with the decision process.
7 Finding a better decision Participants reconsidered whether they could have made a better decision and what it might have been.
Participants determine what change in their decision process could make it more likely that they would reach this better decision in similar situations in the future.

The questions specifically direct them to consider whether it would have been helpful to i) pay less attention to consequences for themselves, ii) pay more attention to consequences for friends and family, ii) pay more attention to consequences for other people they know, iv) pay more attention to consequences for other people they don't know, v) follow the Golden Rule, vi) ensure fairness, vii) follow their moral intuitions about right and wrong, viii) maximize the sum of everyone's well-being, and four other decision strategies.
9 Formulating implementation intentions
Participants formulated an If-Then plan for when to apply this improved decision strategy in similar situations in the future.
After the second decision, participants answered a series of questions about how they had made it.
These questions covered the consequences they considered in making their decision and their decision strategies.
Considered consequences.
Participants were first asked to list all potential consequences they had considered.

Participants then counted how many of the consequences they had listed affected each of four stakeholder groups (themselves, friends and family, acquaintances, and strangers) and rated how important the outcomes for each group had been for their decision on a 7-point scale (with an additional "I didn't think of any such consequences" option scored as 0).

We asked participants to rate how much each of the ten decision strategies listed in Table A1 in Appendix A contributed to their choice on a 6-point scale ranging from not at all to more than anything else.
text.formatted: We asked participants to rate how much each of the ten decision strategies listed in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref> in Appendix A contributed to their choice on a 6-point scale ranging from not at all to more than anything else.

text.text: One of those strategies was utilitarian cost-benefit reasoning ("I wanted to maximize the sum of everyone's wellbeing.").
Participants could also list additional considerations that were important to them.

During the reflection, participants in the SMR condition rated how they felt about their first decision on a bipolar scale from -100 (extremely negatively) to +100 (extremely positively) after analyzing its consequences.
Later during the reflection, they rated their satisfaction with the thought process that led to this decision on a bipolar scale from -100 (completely dissatisfied) to +100 (completely satisfied).
All measures in Experiment 1 were single-item or behavioral; the experiment included no multi-item composite scale.
After providing informed consent, participants read the cover story described above and made a first decision.
Immediately afterward, all participants were shown the outcome of that decision for all affected parties, including both the outgroup and the protagonist's ingroup.
Participants in the SMR condition then completed the systematic moral reflection intervention; while participants in the control condition proceeded directly to the next stage.
After a short break, all participants made a second decision later in the same story and reported how they reached it.
Finally, all participants completed four true/false attention-check questions assessing their comprehension of the scenario, and provided feedback on the study.
Analyses followed the preregistrations and were conducted in R. Exploratory analyses are labeled as such throughout.

We tested the effect of SMR on outgroup prosociality in the second decision using the non-parametric ANCOVA function from the R package sm with an automatically chosen smoothing kernel width (Bowman & Azzalini, 1997).

text.text: We probed the underlying mechanisms with two converging approaches: First, preregistered causal mediation analyses (R package mediation; Tingley et al., 2014; 10,000 bootstrap simulations) tested whether SMR's effect on the second decision was mediated by specified changes in the decision process, controlling for the first decision.
text.formatted: We probed the underlying mechanisms with two converging approaches: First, preregistered causal mediation analyses (R package mediation; <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Tingley et al., 2014</ref>; 10,000 bootstrap simulations) tested whether SMR's effect on the second decision was mediated by specified changes in the decision process, controlling for the first decision.

text.text: Second, we conducted an automatic thematic analysis of the free-text lessons that the SMR-condition participants wrote at the end of their reflection.

In brief, we parsed each response into atomic behavioral and metacognitive lessons, coded them for themes, clustered them into a small set of higher-order themes, and then counted how many themes from each cluster appeared in each participant's lesson (see Section S1.1.1 for the full procedure and prompts).

Exploratory parallel multiple-mediation models (R package lavaan 0.6-19; Rosseel, 2012) tested whether these theme counts mediated the effect of SMR on the second decision, with one mediator per theme cluster (set to zero for controlcondition participants) and the first decision included as a covariate.

text.text: To assess the reliability of the automatic cluster assignments, two independent human coders re-coded all 205 lessons against the fixed cluster definitions.
Critically, both coders were blind to the AI-generated labels and the mediation results.

Within the analytic sample, their codes reproduced the automatic assignments well for every cluster that carried a significant indirect effect (mean human-model κ = .63-.91; inter-coder κ = .88-1.00), supporting the reliability of the mediator measurements (see Sections S1.1.2 and S1.1.3).

Nonparametric procedures have no degrees of freedom: the nonparametric ANCOVAs, the bootstrapped t tests, and the z tests reported for Kendall's τ and for indirect effects are therefore reported without them.
Degrees of freedom are reported for all parametric tests.
Consistent with Prediction 1, systematic moral reflection significantly increased outgroup prosociality in the second decision.

Participants who reflected on their first decision subsequently volunteered about 2.4 hours more (M = 9.5, SD = 6.1) than control participants (M = 7.1, SD = 5.3); the preregistered nonparametric ANCOVA testing equality of the two conditions' regression curves (smoothing bandwidth h = 1.61) confirmed that the difference was statistically significant, p < .001, as did a t test, t(426.58) = 4.44, p < .001, d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.24, 0.62]; see Figure 2A.

text.text: About 81% of participants in the SMR condition reported learning a useful lesson (81.3%).
An automatic thematic analysis identified six clusters of lessons among these participants (n = 178; see Table S2.1.1).

text.text: The most common cluster, present in 59.0% of the lessons, expressed a resolve to prioritize the greater good, strangers, and those in greatest need.

In addition, 38.2% of the lessons expressed a commitment to act prosocially (e.g., to volunteer when needed), 28.1% resolved to decide more deliberately by taking time, gathering information, and weighing trade-offs, and 19.7% invoked ethical principles, empathy, or perspective-taking.

Two smaller clusters ran counter to the outgroup-prosocial direction of the majority: 15.7% of the lessons resolved to set boundaries and protect one's own time and energy, and 7.9% resolved to prioritize or consult one's family.
For the complete definitions of the six clusters, example lessons, and their frequencies, see Section S2.1.1.

Consistent with Predictions 3 and 4, the content of participants' written lessons accounted for most of the effect of systematic moral reflection on the second decision (71.0% mediated, p = .015).
The presence of themes about prioritizing the greater good or strangers who are worse off mediated 31.7% of the effect.
In addition, lessons expressing a commitment to act prosocially mediated 24.0% of the effect, and resolving to decide more deliberately mediated 18.3%.
One theme worked against the effect: resolving to prioritize or consult one's family had a significant negative indirect effect (p = .002).

text.text: Further supporting Predictions 3 and 4, reflection produced parallel shifts in how participants made the second decision, and these shifts mediated the increase in outgroup prosociality.

Reflection on the first decision reduced participants' tendency to prioritize consequences affecting their ingroup over consequences affecting the outgroup in the second decision: SMR decreased the importance participants placed on consequences for friends and family (from M = 4.43 out of 7 in the control condition to M = 3.82 after SMR; t(432.5) = -3.14, p < .001), and this mediated about 17.1% of SMR's effect on outgroup prosociality (p = .002).

text.text: Consistent with the account's second prediction, the affective and evaluative consequences of the first decision predicted how much participants' behavior changed.

To test whether SMR can promote prosocial behaviors beyond volunteering, we conducted a preregistered replication and extension of Experiment 1 with a donation decision (Experiment S1; N = 434, d = 0.31; see Figure 2B and Section S3 of the Supplemental Materials for the full report).
text.formatted: To test whether SMR can promote prosocial behaviors beyond volunteering, we conducted a preregistered replication and extension of Experiment 1 with a donation decision (Experiment S1; N = 434, d = 0.31; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2B</ref> and Section S3 of the Supplemental Materials for the full report).

text.text: Participants took the role of a CEO deciding how much of an unexpected profit to donate to a highly effective charity versus return to their employees.

SMR increased the proportion of the available profit donated in the second decision from 43.1% to 51.9% (d = 0.31, p = .001), even though the second decision involved a different charity serving a different cause.
About 81% of reflecting participants reported learning a useful lesson.
The content of those lessons-especially resolving to prioritize the most vulnerable people in greatest need-fully mediated the effect (67.1% mediated, p = .025).

A finer-grained, consequence-level measure of the decision process showed that SMR led participants to consider more consequences for the outgroup and to assign them greater importance relative to consequences for the ingroup; these attentional changes mediated substantial portions of the effect (21.5% and 36.6%, respectively).

Notably, SMR had no effect on moral universalism (Enke et al., 2022), that is, on how participants allocated money between more and less socially distant strangers in the absence of any information about their needs (all p ≥ .55).
text.formatted: Notably, SMR had no effect on moral universalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Enke et al., 2022)</ref>, that is, on how participants allocated money between more and less socially distant strangers in the absence of any information about their needs (all p ≥ .55).

text.text: The lessons participants learned thus generalized to a new decision benefiting similar people in need but not to impartiality toward strangers in general.
Experiment S1 thereby replicated the support for Predictions 1, 2, 3, and 4 in a new decision domain (see Section S3).
text.formatted: Experiment S1 thereby replicated the support for Predictions 1, 2, 3, and 4 in a new decision domain (see Section <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: In Experiment 1 and its preregistered replication in a donation dilemma (Experiment S1), a single round of systematic moral reflection increased participants' outgroup prosociality in the subsequent decision.

Retrospective self-reports about the decision process and thematic analysis of participants' written lessons converged on the same account: SMR taught participants to deliberate more, to give more weight to potential consequences for distant others, and to place correspondingly less weight on the comparatively minor consequences for themselves and their ingroup.
Those lessons mediated most of the effect.

These results fit the view that moral decision-making is shaped by metacognitive reinforcement learning (Maier et al., 2026; Spiteri, Maier, et al., 2026): a negative verdict on a previous decision shifts one away from the strategy that produced it.
text.formatted: These results fit the view that moral decision-making is shaped by metacognitive reinforcement learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Maier et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Spiteri, Maier, et al., 2026)</ref>: a negative verdict on a previous decision shifts one away from the strategy that produced it.

text.text: Feeling bad about the first decision, and dissatisfied with the strategy behind it, predicted how much the second decision shifted toward helping the outgroup (Prediction 2).

The change was not confined to repeating the same behavior: in Experiment S1, reflecting on a donation to one charity increased giving to a second charity addressing a different cause, suggesting that participants learned a more deliberate, more other-regarding way of deciding rather than a particular behavior.
The change also cannot be reduced to utilitarian cost-benefit reasoning: at least some participants appear to have learned to prioritize those in greatest need.

Consistent with this, SMR increased giving to people in need and to African children at risk of dying from preventable disease, without changing how participants split money between more and less distant others when they have no information about those recipients' needs (see Section S3).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, SMR increased giving to people in need and to African children at risk of dying from preventable disease, without changing how participants split money between more and less distant others when they have no information about those recipients' needs (see Section <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: The following experiments address three limitations of these studies: whether the effects of SMR transfer to other social groups, whether they extend to real, consequential donations, and whether SMR changed behavior by changing feelings and beliefs about the outgroup, as prejudice-reduction interventions are thought to do.
Experiment 2: When Do the Benefits of Systematic Moral Reflection Transfer to Other Usvs-Them Dilemmas Involving Other Social Groups?
Experiment 1 and its supplemental replication (Experiment S1) established that systematic moral reflection can increase outgroup prosociality in volunteering and donation decisions.

However, in each experiment, the outgroup benefiting from the second decision was the same as the outgroup in the first decision (food-insecure Americans in Experiment 1, children in Africa in Experiment S1).

Therefore, Experiment 2 tested whether the increase in outgroup prosociality transfers to another outgroup (sick children receiving surgery) and from one type of decision (volunteering) to another (donating).

In this preregistered experiment, all participants made a volunteering decision, then either went through the systematic moral reflection process (experimental condition) or not (control condition), and finally made a donation decision and completed additional measures.
We recruited 1,547 participants on Prolific Academic.
All participants were Englishspeaking adults located in the USA.
Their ages ranged from 18 to 83 (M = 38.7, SD = 13.24).
Of participants with reported gender, 53.1% were female.
Of the participants with reported ethnicity, 64.4% identified as White, 25.1% as Black, 2.1% as Asian, 5.2% as Mixed, and 3.3% as Other.
Before the main data collection, we decided to reduce the number of attention checks from the four checks mentioned in the pre-registration to two attention checks (one per scenario).
Our rationale was to keep the exclusion rate near 25%, whereas the preregistered criterion would have excluded 37% of participants.
About 77% of the recruited participants (1,195 people) passed both selected attention checks and were included in the subsequent analyses.
These participants were evenly distributed across both conditions (596 in the control condition and 599 in the experimental condition).
A sensitivity analysis confirmed that this deviation did not affect our conclusions (see Table S2.10.1 in the Supplemental Materials)foot_1.
text.formatted: A sensitivity analysis confirmed that this deviation did not affect our conclusions (see Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>.10.1 in the Supplemental Materials)<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref>.

text.text: The procedure for recruiting participants and assigning them to the experimental condition versus the control condition was the same as in the previous experiments.

As preregistered, we aimed to continue data collection until 600 participants in each condition had passed the attention checks; after final data cleaning, slightly fewer analyzable participants remained (596 and 599; see Participants).

Because the effect of interest in this experiment is transfer to a second dilemma involving a different outgroup, we set this target to be sensitive to an effect smaller than the within-domain effects of Experiments 1 and S1.
The attained sample size provides 80% power to detect an effect of d = 0.14 in a one-tailed test at α = .05.
In the experiment, participants first read a fictional scenario, asking them to put themselves in the shoes of an employee of a non-profit organization that provides food to people in need.
They then decided how much of their free time to volunteer to help their organization achieve its goals.
In this decision, participants had to trade off benefits to foodinsecure beneficiaries against costs to themselves and their family and friends.
Then, all participants were informed of the outcome of their decision and answered two attention-check questions.
Next, as in Experiment 1, the participants in the experimental condition engaged in systematic moral reflection.

Next, both groups read a second vignette, asking them to now put themselves in the shoes of an accountant who must decide how much of a holiday bonus check to donate to a local children's hospital or spend on a family vacation to Bali.
In this decision, participants had to trade off the potential benefit to sick, underprivileged children against the benefit to themselves and their families.
This second decision served as our preregistered measure of the transfer of the intervention's effect on prosociality toward a different outgroup.

Finally, all participants reported on how they reached their decision, answered additional questions measuring social discounting, moral expansiveness, and impartial beneficence, and completed two further attention checks and a comprehension-confirmation item.
The first social dilemma pitted the needs of a large outgroup (i.e., food-insecure individuals) against the interests of a charity worker, their family, and their friends.
Participants entered this dilemma as the charity worker.
They first read a description of the charity's activities and the charity worker's general life circumstances and work environment (see Section S5.3.1).
The description specified that the charity provides meals to food-insecure people in the local community.
It also specified that the charity worker has three children and splits the childcare responsibilities equally with their spouse.
The scenario description also noted that the charity operates under tight constraints and is sometimes short-staffed.

In this volunteering dilemma, each participant decided how many hours they would volunteer in the second week of April to help the charity achieve its goals despite the illness of a co-worker (see Section S5.3).
Participants reported their decision by dragging a slider over a range from 0 hours to 20 hours in 1-hour increments.
The second social dilemma (see Section S5.3.2) pitted the needs of a local children's hospital against the interests of an accountant and their family.

In the shoes of an accountant who was awarded a $4,995 holiday bonus check for excellent work completed that year, participants had the choice to donate to the local children's hospital to help fund new surgical equipment or spend it on booking a family vacation to Bali.
Participants again responded on a slider ranging from $0 donated (and everything to the family vacation) to $4,995 donated (and nothing to the family vacation).
Each social dilemma was illustrated with images generated with DALL-E 3 (OpenAI, 2023) from prompts describing the scenario depicted in the corresponding vignette.
The authors selected the final images and used them without further modification.
The Socratic questions of the systematic reflection intervention comprised the same nine steps as in Experiments 1 and S1 (see Table 2).
text.formatted: The Socratic questions of the systematic reflection intervention comprised the same nine steps as in Experiments 1 and S1 (see Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: However, we made slight enhancements to was split up into a series of questions that guided participants to i) find a way of thinking (strategy) that can help them avoid the mistake they reflected on, ii) to identify future situations where this strategy can help them make better decisions, and iii) formulate an If-Then plan to apply the chosen strategy in the relevant situations.

Participants then reported how soon they would implement the lesson and answered a series of Likert-scale questions about the usefulness of the lesson they created and their likelihood of implementing it in real life.
Assessment of the considered consequences.
Following the second decision, participants answered a series of questions about their decision process.
To ground participants' ratings in what they actually considered during the decision process, we first asked them to list which potential outcomes they considered while making their second decision.
We also presented participants with a list of morally significant potential consequences affecting the outgroup and asked them to indicate which they had considered.
We then asked participants to rate the consequences on a series of dimensions.
These questions were similar to those of Experiments 1 and S1, except that they also assessed the moral significance of self-generated consequences.
Specifically, we measured the following factors for each considered consequence:
Importance.
Participants rated how important each consequence had been for their decision on a scale from 0-100.
Participants rated how good or bad each consequence would be on a scale from -100 to 100.
We calculated each consequence's extremity as the absolute value of this rating.
Participants chose which group the consequence affected.
Participants rated the likelihood of the consequence by predicting how many times it would occur if they took the same action 100 times, on a 0-100 scale.
Participants entered a single number indicating how many people they thought the consequence would affect.
Participants rated the change in well-being by assessing how much happier or unhappier those affected would be, on a scale of -10 to 10.
Participants indicated how long the change in well-being would last by completing a form field comprising a unit of time and a number.

We calculated the moral significance of each reported consequence by multiplying its likelihood by the number of people affected, the well-being change per person affected, and the duration of this effect.
Following Nguyen et al. (2026), we categorized a consequence as morally significant if this product was equal to or greater than 0.37 well-beingadjusted life years.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Nguyen et al. (2026)</ref>, we categorized a consequence as morally significant if this product was equal to or greater than 0.37 well-beingadjusted life years.

text.text: We measured how much participants had relied on moral intuition, deliberation, moral rules, and cost-benefit reasoning when making the second decision using the 12-item Decision Process Scale developed by Cheung et al. (2026) on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 100 (entirely).

(2026)</ref> on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 100 (entirely).

text.text: Participants could also list additional considerations that were important to them.

Participants were presented with a list of individuals from various social groups, comprising a family member, a close friend, a coworker, a community member, an elderly community member, a special needs community member, a children's hospital patient in the community (the outgroup in the second decision), and a complete stranger.
Participants were asked to place each individual in one of the four circles of moral concern from the moral expansiveness scale (Crimston et al., 2016)

text.text: This task first asks participants to list the first, second, fifth, tenth, twentieth, and fiftieth closest people to them.
Participants then make a series of seven allocation http://decisions.in/.

text.text: In the first six allocation decisions, they allocated $10 between themselves and one of the individuals they had listed.
In the last allocation decision, they allocated $10 between themselves and a member of the outgroup in the second decision.
Participants rated their agreement with the 5 statements of the impartial beneficence sub-scale of the Oxford Utilitarianism Scale (Kahane et al., 2018).

text.text: All other measures in this experiment were single-item or behavioral.
The attention checks comprised four true-or-false questions about the two social dilemmas.
The first two followed the first social dilemma decision, and the final two followed the measures asking participants how they had reached the second decision.

A fifth true-or-false item, asking participants to confirm that the consequences they had listed referred only to the second decision, served as a comprehension confirmation and was not used for exclusions.
We preregistered the data analysis at https://aspredicted.org/cgd2-qp42.pdf.

text.text: We tested between-group differences in moral concern with bootstrapped t-tests using 10,000 resamples, which we report without degrees of freedom.

To statistically identify lesson types that promote outgroup prosociality, we conducted causal mediation analyses using bootstrapping with 10,000 simulations with the mediation package in R (Tingley et al., 2014).

text.text: All mediation analyses controlled for individual differences in the first decision.

Consistent with Predictions 1 and 5, the effect of systematic moral reflection on a volunteering decision transferred to donations supporting a different outgroup: systematic reflection significantly increased the amount donated to charity in the second decision relative to the control condition (h = 0.0851, p < .001; see Figure 2C and Figure S2.7.2 in the Supplemental Materials).

text.text: After reflecting on the outcomes of the initial volunteering decision and how it would affect each group in question, participants in the experimental condition decided to donate $501.92 more to a local children's hospital than the control group: donations increased from $1,914.91 in the control condition (M = $1,914.91, SD = $1,302.31) to $2,416.83 in the experimental condition (M = $2,416.83, SD = $1,396.39; t(1188) = -6.43, p < .001; d = 0.37, 95% CI [0.26, 0.49]).

text.text: We found strong evidence of transfer effects to the three other measures of outgroup prosociality: social discounting, moral concern for distant others, and impartial beneficence.

Systematic moral reflection significantly increased participants' average level of moral concern for non-close others (i.e., the six targets other than their family member and their close friend; M = 1.70, SD = 0.57) compared to those who did not go through the reflection (M = 1.60, SD = 0.55; t = 3.23, p = .002; d = 0.19, 95% CI [0.07, 0.30]), including the sick children from the second dilemma (t = 3.50, p = .001; d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.09, 0.32]).

Systematic moral reflection also increased participants' endorsement of the moral principle of impartial beneficence (t(1190.6) = 3.25, p = .001; d = 0.19, 95% CI [0.07, 0.30]) from 4.01 out of 7 in the control group (SD = 1.34) to 4.26 out of 7 in the experimental group (SD = 1.29).

Moreover, the rate at which participants' discounting of the welfare of others increased with their social distance was significantly lower for participants who had engaged in systematic reflection (log(k) = -5.74) than for the control group (log(k) = -5.27), b = -0.47, SE = 0.12, t(7168) = -4.08, p < .001.
text.formatted: Moreover, the rate at which participants' discounting of the welfare of others increased with their social distance was significantly lower for participants who had engaged in systematic reflection (log(k) = -5.74) than for the control group (log(k) = -5.27), b = -0.47, SE = 0.12, t(7168) = -4.08, p < .001.

text.text: In an exploratory follow-up analysis, we asked whether these changes in participants' moral concern and endorsement of impartial beneficence could account for the increase in donations.

We found that they could not fully account for it, although they accounted for part of it: adjusting simultaneously for moral concern for the sick children, moral concern for the six non-close targets, and impartial beneficence reduced the effect of systematic moral reflection on the amount donated from b = 502.91 to b = 375.31, which remained significant, t(1189) = 5.21, p < .001 (see Table S2.9.5).

text.text: Because these measures were assessed after the second decision, this analysis bounds rather than identifies the mechanism, and because Experiment 2 included no measure of participants' feelings toward the outgroup, it speaks only to their beliefs.
Experiment 3 tests this question with a fuller set of measures.
As part of the systematic moral reflection, participants rated how much different strategies could have helped them reach a better decision.

The average participant reported that relying more on cost-benefit reasoning would have been more helpful than not (M = 1.82, SD = 1.23, t(598) = 36.27, p < .001), and that paying more attention to outcomes for people they don't know would be more helpful (M = 1.37, SD = 1.41) than paying more attention to outcomes for their friends and family (M = 0.89, SD = 1.45; paired t(598) = 6.17, p < .001; dz = 0.25, 95% CI [0.17, 0.33]).

text.text: Consistent with these findings, our automatic thematic analysis of the lessons participants wrote down at the end of their systematic moral reflection found that, of all participants in the experimental condition, 57.6% learned a lesson endorsing deliberative, evidence-based decision-making, 33.9% learned a lesson endorsing impartial beneficence or the prioritization of vulnerable others even if they are distant, 24.9% learned a lesson about prioritizing their family or setting boundaries to protect their own well-being, 22.0% resolved to involve other members of their organization/community in the decision or decide according to their preferences, 21.4% learned a lesson endorsing an ethical principle or moral constraint, and 6.2% of participants learned a lesson endorsing continuous improvement, learning from feedback, or reflection (see Table S2.1.3 for details).

text.text: Participants in the experimental group rated the lessons they wrote down at the end of the reflection as useful for making better decisions (M = 1.53 on a scale from -2 to +2, SD = 0.48, t(540) = 73.64, p < .001) and reported that they were likely to use them in similar social dilemmas (M = 1.58 on a scale from -2 to +2, SD = 0.55, t(543) = 66.38, p < .001).

text.text: Our parallel mediation analysis found that the presence of the six types of themes in the lessons participants wrote down (see Table S2.1.3) mediated about 38.5% (95% CI [10.1%, 79.1%]) of the effect of systematic moral reflection.

text.text: As in Experiment 1, two independent human coders, who were blind to the model's assignments and to the mediation results, re-coded a random sample of 150 lessons from the analytic sample against the fixed cluster definitions.

Their codes reproduced the automatic assignments well for the cluster that carried the significant indirect effect (impartial beneficence; mean Cohen's κ = .64 against the LLM, with inter-coder agreement of κ = .79), supporting the reliability of the mediator measurement (see Sections S1.1.4 and S1.1.5 of the Supplemental Materials).

Analyzing how participants made the second decision revealed that systematic moral reflection induced several related changes in participants' decision strategies that contributed to the increase in outgroup prosociality.
Several of these changes were consistent with people learning to give more consideration to vulnerable/distant others and become more impartial.

Consistent with Predictions 3 and 4, exploratory mediation analyses indicated that three types of strategies participants reported using in the second decision mediated a significant proportion of the reflection-induced increase in outgroup prosociality.

In the second decision, the experimental group reported striving to behave like a virtuous person or moral saint to a greater extent (M = 3.38, SD = 1.47) than the control group (M = 3.03, SD = 1.61; t(1182.1) = -3.87, p < .001; d = 0.22, 95% CI [0.11, 0.34]).
text.formatted: In the second decision, the experimental group reported striving to behave like a virtuous person or moral saint to a greater extent (M = 3.38, SD = 1.47) than the control group (M = 3.03, SD = 1.61; t(1182.1) = -3.87, p < .001; d = 0.22, 95% CI [0.11, 0.34]).

text.text: This mediated about 27.0% of the effect of systematic moral reflection on outgroup prosociality.

Similarly, the experimental group reported relying more on the Golden Rule ("Treat others the way you want to be treated"; M = 3.51, SD = 1.36) than the control group (M = 3.22, SD = 1.55; t(1172.4) = -3.46, p = .001; d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.09, 0.31]).
This mediated about 23.7% of the effect of systematic reflection on outgroup prosociality.

Finally, the experimental group wanted to ensure fairness significantly more (M = 3.61, SD = 1.2) than the control group (M = 3.40, SD = 1.29; t(1185.8) = -2.84, p = .005; d = 0.16, 95% CI [0.05, 0.28]).
This explained about 17.5% of the effect of systematic moral reflection on outgroup prosociality.

According to the Decision Process Scale, there was a significant decrease in reliance on moral intuition for those who went through the reflection (M = 71.67, SD = 18.69) compared to those who didn't (M = 73.99, SD = 17.83; t(1190.9) = -2.19, p = .029; d = -0.13, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.01]); however, it was not found to be a significant mediator to outgroup prosociality.
Participants' self-reported reliance on deliberation, moral rules, and costbenefit reasoning was unaffected (all ps ≥ .100; see Table S2.11.1).

text.text: Mediation by increased attention to outgroup consequences.

Systematic reflection significantly increased the number of outgroup consequences participants considered in the second decision from 3.83 in the control group (SD = 2.39) to 4.43 in the experimental group (SD = 2.44; t(1192.7) = -4.24, p < .001; d = 0.25, 95% CI [0.13, 0.36]).

text.text: We found that this increase in participants' attention to outgroup consequences mediated 26.1% of the effect of the reflection on how much money they donated in the second decision (95% CI [15.1%, 40%], p < .001).
text.formatted: We found that this increase in participants' attention to outgroup consequences mediated 26.1% of the effect of the reflection on how much money they donated in the second decision (95% CI [15.1%, 40%], p < .001).

text.text: The indirect effect of the reflection on money donated through an increase in considered outgroup consequences was $131.30 (95% CI [$70.01, $195.10], p < .001).

text.text: Moreover, as predicted, SMR also increased the number of morally significant consequences participants considered in the second decision from 5.59 in the control group (SD = 3.49) to 6.01 in the experimental group (SD = 3.46; t(1192.8) = -2.09, p = .037; d = 0.12, 95% CI [0.01, 0.23]).

This increase mediated 13.1% of the effect of the reflection on how much money they donated to help the outgroup (95% CI [1.4%, 25.0%], p = .031; indirect effect = $66.04, 95% CI [$6.73, $128.13]; see Table S2.6.3 in the Supplemental Materials).

text.text: Systematic reflection significantly increased the relative importance the experimental group assigned to outgroup consequences (M = 7.33, SD = 22.31) relative to the control group (M = 3.71, SD = 20.68; t(860.99) = -2.48, p = .007), as measured by the difference between the importance ratings of the most important outgroup consequence and the most important ingroup consequence.

We found that 15.32% of the effect of systematic reflection on money donated to help the outgroup was mediated by an increase in the relative importance of the decision's effects on the outgroup (95% CI [3.47%, 28.73%], p = .011).
The indirect effect on money donated through an increase in the relative importance of outgroup outcomes was $73.33 (95% CI [$14.98, $133.14], p = .011; see Table S2.6.3).

The indirect effect through an increase in impartial beneficence was $90.68 (95% CI [35.98, 151.52], p = .001; see Table S2.6.3).

text.text: This corroborates the earlier finding that systematic moral reflection was mediated by participants learning moral lessons related to impartial beneficence.
The experimental group's increased moral concern for the outgroup of the second dilemma, mediated 14.13% of the effect of the reflection on subsequent donations (95% CI [6.16%, 24.22%], p = .001).

text.text: Experiment 2 showed that the benefits of systematic moral reflection can extend to a second dilemma involving a different outgroup.
A further preregistered experiment (Experiment S2; N = 966) identified a boundary condition for the breadth of this transfer effect.
text.formatted: A further preregistered experiment (Experiment <ref type="table">S2</ref>; N = 966) identified a boundary condition for the breadth of this transfer effect.

text.text: Experiment S2 used the same first decision as Experiments 1 and 2, but changed the structure of the second social dilemma.

In the first decision, participants traded off their own and their family's time against the needs of food-insecure people in their community, and those assigned to the experimental condition then completed the same systematic moral reflection.

All participants subsequently took the role of a CEO deciding how to allocate $194,725 of unexpected profit between a Christmas bonus for the company's 100 employees (and themselves) and a donation to Helen Keller International, a charity that treats vitamin A deficiency in young children in Africa.
This second dilemma differed from the one used in Experiment 2 in several important ways.

First, unlike in Experiment 2, where the ingroup remained the same, Experiment S2's second decision replaced the protagonist's family with a new group of less well-off people outside of the protagonist's family.
Second, the outgroup changed from fellow Americans to children in Africa.
The full method and results are reported in Section S4 of the Supplemental Materials.
For the pair of social dilemmas used in Experiment S2, SMR had no detectable effect on this second decision.

Participants who reflected donated about the same amount (M = $70,720, SD = $51,200) as participants who did not (M = $71,150, SD = $45,570), t(940.73) = -0.14, p = .889, d = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.12] (Figure 2D).
text.formatted: Participants who reflected donated about the same amount (M = $70,720, SD = $51,200) as participants who did not (M = $71,150, SD = $45,570), t(940.73) = -0.14, p = .889, d = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.12] (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2D</ref>).

text.text: The preregistered nonparametric ANCOVA also found no difference between the two conditions' regression curves (h = 0.09, p = .992), and an exploratory test found no evidence that the curves were not parallel (h = 0.09, p = .966).
This null result does not reflect insufficient power.

With 966 participants the design had 80% power to detect an effect of d = 0.18 in a two-tailed test, and the confidence interval excludes the effects observed in Experiment 1 (d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.24, 0.62]), Experiment S1 (d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.12, 0.50]) and Experiment 2 (d = 0.37, 95% CI [0.26, 0.48]).
In fact, there was no overlap between the confidence intervals of Experiments 2 and S2.
The intervention of Experiment S2 engaged participants as it did in Experiments 1 and 2.

Of those in the SMR condition, 77.6% reported having learned a useful lesson, a rate comparable to Experiments 1 and 2, and the lessons they reported were no less relevant to the second decision: 61.3% expressed an orientation toward impartial altruism and the greater good, and 67.6% were general resolutions about how to decide rather than what to do (Table S4.1).
