text.text: This suggests the bottleneck in transfer was not learning useful lessons but applying them to a new kind of scenario.
Moreover, the learning signal itself operated as predicted (Prediction 2): the worse participants felt about their first decision, the more their second decision changed (see Section S4).
We return to this in the Discussion below.

In Experiment 2, reflecting on how they had treated one outgroup increased participants' prosociality toward a different outgroup, via greater moral concern for the outgroup, stronger endorsement of the principle of impartial beneficence, and corresponding changes in the strategies they used to make the second social dilemma decision.

Once again, participants' decisions, attitudes, process-tracing data, and written lessons converged on the same conclusion: SMR taught people to consider more ways in which their decisions might affect the outgroup and to take those effects more seriously.
While Experiment 2 demonstrated a transfer effect, the absence of transfer in Experiment S2 indicates that its scope is limited.
The two experiments differed only in the second decision, and in Experiment S2 that decision changed both the outgroup and the ingroup.
We return to what this implies about the boundary of transfer in the General Discussion, after integrating the results of Experiment 3.
Relations on a Real Social Issue Experiments 1, S1, 2, and S2 measured outgroup prosociality via hypothetical decisions.
This experiment addresses this limitation by showing that SMR can motivate people to engage in costly helping of a stigmatized social group in the real world.

Concretely, we test whether SMR can increase how much real money people donate to help transgender individuals and immigrants, and how it affects the affective and cognitive components of their attitudes toward these groups.

Prior research has evaluated a range of interventions for reducing prejudice against transgender people (Flores et al., 2021; Tompkins et al., 2015), including some that have backfired among members of dominant groups (Flores et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Prior research has evaluated a range of interventions for reducing prejudice against transgender people <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Flores et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Tompkins et al., 2015)</ref>, including some that have backfired among members of dominant groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Flores et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This motivates both developing more effective interventions and evaluating them more thoroughly-the two goals Experiment 3 pursues.
SMR is designed to foster moral learning, which can produce lasting moral change.
Experiments 1, S1, 2, and S2 measured only the intervention's immediate effects, leaving it unclear whether SMR's effects were fleeting or lasting.
Experiment 3 tests whether they last for at least one week and, in a second follow-up, whether they are still detectable about four and a half months later.

A further question is whether SMR, which takes more time and effort, has any benefits over perspective taking and empathy induction, two approaches that are thoroughly established in the social psychology literature (e.g., Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997; Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000).
text.formatted: A further question is whether SMR, which takes more time and effort, has any benefits over perspective taking and empathy induction, two approaches that are thoroughly established in the social psychology literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: While those interventions promote compassion toward a specific outgroup (e.g., Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997), SMR teaches people to weigh the impact of their decisions on any distant stranger more heavily.
text.formatted: While those interventions promote compassion toward a specific outgroup (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997)</ref>, SMR teaches people to weigh the impact of their decisions on any distant stranger more heavily.

text.text: By increasing the weight assigned to others' welfare in general rather than inducing feeling toward one group, SMR might make people more prosocial toward groups that were never the focus of reflection.

This differentiates SMR from empathy induction through perspective-taking, which has been found to motivate people to help one person or group at the expense of the greater good (e.g., Batson, Batson, et al., 1995; Batson, Klein, et al., 1995).
text.formatted: This differentiates SMR from empathy induction through perspective-taking, which has been found to motivate people to help one person or group at the expense of the greater good (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Batson, Batson, et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batson, Klein, et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore predict that SMR will be uniquely effective at improving the effectiveness of people's donations, more likely to transfer to decisions about helping other outgroups, and less likely to make people prefer ineffective help for transgender individuals over highly effective charities helping other groups.

To evaluate SMR against the two state-of-the-art interventions for reducing prejudice against an outgroup and a neutral control group, we conducted a preregistered multi-arm pretest-posttest randomized controlled trial.
We measured the effectiveness of each intervention both immediately after its delivery and in two follow-up assessments, at least 7 days and about four and a half months later.
We preregistered the experimental procedure and data analysis at https://aspredicted.org/zn7ie7.pdf for the immediate effects and at https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf for the follow-up effects.
text.formatted: We preregistered the experimental procedure and data analysis at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/zn7ie7.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/zn7ie7.pdf</ref> for the immediate effects and at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf</ref> for the follow-up effects.

text.text: The second follow-up (Part 3) was designed and pre-registered after Part 2 (https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf).
text.formatted: The second follow-up (Part 3) was designed and pre-registered after Part 2 (<ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf</ref>).

text.text: In addition to asking people to deliberate, SMR also guides them to take the perspective of the outgroup members they have helped or harmed and to empathize with them.

Previous work has shown that perspective taking and empathy induction are sufficient to promote outgroup prosociality on their own (e.g., Adida et al., 2018; Batson, Sager, et al., 1997; Clore & Jeffery, 1972; Dovidio et al., 2004; Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000; Johnson, 1967; Rodríguez Chatruc & Rozo, 2024; Simonovits et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Previous work has shown that perspective taking and empathy induction are sufficient to promote outgroup prosociality on their own (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Adida et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Batson, Sager, et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Clore & Jeffery, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Dovidio et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Johnson, 1967;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Rodríguez Chatruc & Rozo, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Simonovits et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These interventions have been found to be effective across a wide range of outgroups (Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997; Todd & Galinsky, 2014), including transgender people (Flores et al., 2021; Tompkins et al., 2015) and immigrants (Adida et al., 2018; Rodríguez Chatruc & Rozo, 2024).
text.formatted: These interventions have been found to be effective across a wide range of outgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Batson, Polycarpou, et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Todd & Galinsky, 2014)</ref>, including transgender people <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Flores et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Tompkins et al., 2015)</ref> and immigrants <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adida et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Rodríguez Chatruc & Rozo, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We aimed to recruit 2,400 adult participants on Prolific (600 per condition).

For ethical and scientific reasons, we used Prolific's screening function to restrict participation to adult US citizens residing in the US who are fluent in English, do not identify as LGBTQ+, and have an approval rate of at least 95% on Prolific.
Our rationale for the target sample size was as follows.
Anticipating that effects diminish over time, we aimed for 80% power to detect effects of d = 0.14 or larger at α = .05 in one-sided tests, adjusting for each outcome's pre-intervention value.
Using pilot data, we estimated that the correlation between pre-and post-intervention scores would be at least 0.61.
With these inputs, ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2025-2026) calculated that we would need about 400 analyzable participants per condition.
We recruited 600 per condition to allow for data-quality exclusions and for attrition at the one-week follow-up.

Due to a technical error, the systematic moral reflection (SMR) materials did not display correctly to the 69 participants who entered that condition during the first two days of data collection; we detected and corrected the error on the second collection day.
Because these participants did not receive the intended manipulation, we excluded their data from all analyses; we compensated them in full, and we recruited replacement participants.
Part 1.
In total, 2,493 participants entered the Part 1 survey after the error was corrected.
Following the preregistered criteria, 62 participants who identified as transgender or as unsure/questioning were screened out, and seven ended the survey before random assignment.

Of the 2,424 randomized participants who completed the survey, 114 were excluded for failing more than one of three attention and comprehension checks, completing the survey in less than one-third of their condition's median completion time, or not being confidently classified as unassisted human respondents by Prolific's authenticity checks;
Section S1.6 of the Supplemental Materials details the checks, pass rates, and exclusion cascade.
Participants who endorsed false descriptions of the charities' aims (pass rate 67.9%) were additionally excluded from all donation analyses.

The final Part 1 analytic sample comprised 2,310 participants (582 SMR, 574 neutral reflection, 596 empathy induction, 558 perspective taking), of whom 1,217 were women and 1,093 were men (mean age 37.2 years, SD = 12.5, range 18-106).

Based on Prolific's demographic records, 65.1% of participants were White, 16.9% Black, 7.4% of mixed ethnicity, 6.3% Asian, and 3.1% from other ethnicities (1.2% unavailable or undisclosed); all resided in the United States, 91.9% were born there, and 45.1% were employed full-time.
The final longitudinal sample comprised 2,007 participants who met the preregistered criteria in both parts (EI: n = 521; SMR: n = 504; NR: n = 497; PT: n = 485).
Missing follow-up data were not imputed.

Retention exceeded the target of 400 analyzable participants per condition, and the observed correlation between pre-intervention and follow-up donations was r = .70, higher than the value assumed when planning the sample size.
As a result, the realized power exceeded the planned level.
We preregistered that Part 1 data collection would continue until 2400 participants had completed the first survey or until 14 days after launch, whichever came first.
We invited each participant who completed Part 1 to Part 2 seven days later.
As preregistered, Part 2 data collection closed 7 days after the last Part 1 participants were invited to Part 2.
After providing informed consent, participants were asked whether they identified as transgender and whether they identified as an immigrant in the USA.

We then measured the baseline values of several key dependent variables: positive/negative feelings toward transgender people and immigrants, welfare-tradeoff ratios, and donation-based measures of i) outgroup prosociality, ii) outgroup hostility, and iii) effectiveness focus.
Participants then received their condition-specific intervention.

We measured empathic concern for transgender people immediately after each intervention (empathy induction, perspective taking, neutral reflection) or after the part of the intervention designed to induce empathic concern (SMR).
Next, participants completed the postintervention measures.
The first set of post-intervention measures was the two donation-based measures with an equivalent set of different charities.
Participants then rated their feelings toward transgender people and immigrants again (feeling thermometers; Tyler & Iyengar, 2024).
text.formatted: Participants then rated their feelings toward transgender people and immigrants again (feeling thermometers; <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Tyler & Iyengar, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Next, they were presented with a Likert scale measuring their support for pro-and anti-transgender policies (policy support).
After that, participants indicated how (un)willing they would be to engage in different types of social relationships with transgender people and immigrants (stigma).
The following scales measured participants' post-intervention welfaretradeoff ratios and moral concern for the two outgroups.
The survey's final measures were selfother overlap with members of the two outgroups, impartial beneficence, and blatant dehumanization (see Measures for details).
Each participant who completed their first survey was invited to the follow-up survey 7 days later.

The follow-up survey included the feeling thermometers from Part 1, welfare tradeoff ratio measures for transgender people and immigrants, new sets of donation decisions measuring outgroup prosociality, outgroup hostility, and effectiveness focus, along with measures of their support for policies protecting transgender people, stigma against transgender people and immigrants, moral concern for transgender people, perceived self-other overlap with transgender people and immigrants, blatant dehumanization of transgender people and immigrants, and impartial beneficence.
The second follow-up survey (Part 3) was titled "Decisions about Money and Time, Part 3" and did not mention transgender people, immigrants, or the earlier intervention.
It remained open for 14 days, with one reminder, and paid $5.00 (median completion time: about 15 minutes).
To minimize reactivity, behavior was measured before attitudes.
Participants first made three incentive-compatible donation decisions.
Each time, they decided how much money to donate to a charity ($0-$100) if they won the experiment's $100 raffle.
The three charities supported transgender people, victims of natural disasters, or the arts, respectively.

Participants then made three allocation decisions in which they split money between a charity helping transgender people and another charity focussed on three other causes (arts and culture, disaster victims, and the participant's local community).
None of the charities in Part 3 had been used in Part 1 or Part 2.
Participants then completed the welfare tradeoff ratio measures, the blatant dehumanization scale, the feeling thermometers, and the willingness-to-interact scale from Parts 1 and 2.

Next, they could take two real prosocial actions: adding their name to a collective letter of support for transgender people and writing a supportive note for delivery to a transgender person through a nonprofit letter-writing program.

Finally, they placed transgender people, LGB people, immigrants, and members of their immediate family in their moral circle separately for four types of moral concern, beginning with the obligation to help them (positive obligations), and completed a funnel debriefing about the purpose of the study.

Because the Prolific study initially linked to an outdated draft of the survey, 80 participants (6%) first completed a version that did not record the welfare tradeoff ratios; Section S1.7.3 of the Supplemental Materials describes how we handled this, and Section S1.7 reports the full methods of Part 3.
The full text of the social dilemma scenario used in this experiment is provided in Section S5.4 of the Supplemental Materials.

The systematic moral reflection prompts were identical to those used in Experiment 2, except that the prompts guiding participants to empathize with the people who were most significantly affected by their decision were reworded.
The rewording helped participants take the perspective of those helped or harmed by their decision and then step out of it afterward to reduce empathic distress.
These changes were informed by prior research on the complementary effects of imagining how another person feels versus how oneself would feel in their situation (Batson, Early, et al., 1997).
text.formatted: These changes were informed by prior research on the complementary effects of imagining how another person feels versus how oneself would feel in their situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Batson, Early, et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Table 3 describes the revised perspective-taking prompts in detail.

text.text: Table 3 Prompts Guiding Participants to Assess the Outcomes for the Person Who Was Harmed the Most as Used in the SMR Condition of Experiment 3 1 Now picture this person or one of these people (NAME).
Please describe the negative impact(s) they experienced (e.g., how they were harmed), the situation they were in when it happened, and how it is affecting them now.
Try to describe this in terms of their life and circumstances (e.g., "When Kyle arrived at the food bank at noon, it was closed.
A sign said that today's opening hours had been shortened to 8-11 a.m. because staff are ill and volunteers cancelled.
It took him two hours to walk there.
He hasn't eaten in two days.
He lost his job two months ago, and the food bank was his last hope for feeding his family this weekend.").
Now imagine that you are in the situation of this individual and that the same bad things are happening to you.
We will ask you a few questions as if you were in that situation.
This is just to help you understand what this kind of situation would be like from the inside.
(This prompt and the following question still refer to NAME.).
How does the negative impact of the event you described above relate to your wants and needs?
(Please answer as if you were in this situation yourself; for instance, "The food bank being closed meant that I had to survive on tap water and salt for the third day in a row.
It meant being denied even the most basic thing I need to survive.
It also meant being unable to feed my family for three days in a row, watching them starve, and feeling like a complete failure.") 4
What thoughts are going through your mind as this bad thing is happening to you?
(Please answer as if you were in this situation yourself.) 5
How does this bad event make you feel emotionally?
(Please answer as if you were in this situation yourself.) 6
Now gently let go of imagining yourself in that situation and return your attention to your actual life in the present moment.
From this safe vantage point, we'll focus again on the person in the scenario (NAME).
Note.
The prompts for guiding people to assess their action's effect on those who benefited the most were equivalent.
The word NAME is a placeholder for the name the participant used to describe the person who was most negatively affected by their decision.

In Experiments 1, S1, 2, and S2, the control condition was chosen to assess the degree to which SMR boosts what people learn from the outcome of a social dilemma decision compared with what they would learn without any support.
As a result, the SMR condition was longer than the control condition and included several elements the control condition did not.
The present experiment addresses these limitations with a time-matched neutral reflection condition that controls for duration, difficulty, and deliberation.
Controlling for time and difficulty eliminates potential confounds due to self-selection, drop-out, or exhaustion.
Controlling for reflection helps distinguish the unique effects of systematic moral reflection from merely shifting people from intuitive to deliberative processing (Rand & Epstein, 2014).
text.formatted: Controlling for reflection helps distinguish the unique effects of systematic moral reflection from merely shifting people from intuitive to deliberative processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Rand & Epstein, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The neutral reflection prompts asked participants to reflect on enjoyable everyday activities.

The prompts were designed to match the amount of reflection, time, and writing required by the SMR intervention without evoking reflection on either morally relevant outcomes or decision-making processes.
Participants first listed four everyday activities they find enjoyable and selected two of them to reflect on.

For each of the two activities, participants answered seventeen questions about the activity, including where, when, and how they engage in it, how they experience it, how it fits into their life, and the last time they engaged in it.
Afterward, participants answered seven questions about how the two activities are similar, how they are different, and how they complement each other.
Following Galinsky and Moskowitz (2000), the perspective-taking intervention was framed as testing people's ability to construct life event details from visual information.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Galinsky and Moskowitz (2000)</ref>, the perspective-taking intervention was framed as testing people's ability to construct life event details from visual information.

text.text: Participants were shown an image of a transgender woman with pink hair in a thinking posture sitting on a couch in front of a designer table with a laptop, pencils, paper, and a cellphone. 3Participants were then asked to write a brief passage describing a typical day in the life of the individual in the photograph from a first-person perspective.
text.formatted: Participants were shown an image of a transgender woman with pink hair in a thinking posture sitting on a couch in front of a designer table with a laptop, pencils, paper, and a cellphone. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">3</ref>Participants were then asked to write a brief passage describing a typical day in the life of the individual in the photograph from a first-person perspective.

text.text: They were instructed to try to take the perspective of the photographed individual by going through a typical day in their shoes, as if they were that person.
Participants were prompted to write about the woman's goals and intentions as well as her thoughts and feelings.
They were required to write at least 500 characters (about 100 words) before they could proceed to the next page.

On the next page, participants rated to what extent they had imagined the woman's thoughts and feelings, to what extent they had been objective and detached while writing the essay, and to what extent they used AI to write the passage.
Of the 655 participants assigned to the perspective-taking condition, 608 (92.8%) completed the writing exercise and the subsequent self-reports; their passages averaged 148.7 words (SD = 47.2).

Participants reported having imagined the woman's thoughts and feelings to a considerable degree (M = 4.12, SD = 1.43, on a scale from 0 to 6), with 70.2% giving a rating of 4 or higher and only 1.8% reporting that they had not done so at all.
They reported having been objective and detached to a significantly lesser degree (M = 2.90, SD = 1.86), t(607) = 13.04, p < .001, dz = 0.53.
text.formatted: They reported having been objective and detached to a significantly lesser degree (M = 2.90, SD = 1.86), t(607) = 13.04, p < .001, dz = 0.53.

text.text: Self-reported use of AI was rare: 94.7% reported none at all, and only 2.8% reported using it moderately or more.

Participants therefore engaged with the perspective-taking instructions largely as intended, and the comparison between SMR and perspective taking is unlikely to be attributable to a failure of the perspectivetaking manipulation.
Participants watched a short video (1:17 min) in which a transgender woman is interviewed about being bullied in school 4 .
Prior to watching the video, they were instructed to "try to imagine how the person being interviewed feels about what has happened and how it has affected their life."
Afterward, they were asked to write a paragraph about how the transgender woman interviewed in the video must have felt when she was bullied.
To enforce engagement with these prompts, participants had to spend at least 100 seconds on the page and had to enter at least 20 characters.
The wording of the instructions closely followed the well- 4 The video we used is available in the project's OSF repository.
established empathy induction method by Batson, Polycarpou, et al. (1997) and its adaptation to videos by Dovidio et al. (2004).
text.formatted: established empathy induction method by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batson, Polycarpou, et al. (1997)</ref> and its adaptation to videos by <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Dovidio et al. (2004)</ref>.

text.text: To ensure that participants heard the sound of the video, we required them to pass a sound check before proceeding to the empathy induction intervention.
The sound check required them to correctly report the order in which a low tone, a high tone, and a mid-frequency tone were played.
The order of these tones was randomized.
The JavaScript implementing the sound check was written with ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2025 (OpenAI, -2026) ) and was tested by the authors before data collection.
text.formatted: The JavaScript implementing the sound check was written with ChatGPT <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(OpenAI, 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr">(OpenAI, -2026) )</ref> and was tested by the authors before data collection.

text.text: We selected this video from seven candidates in a pilot study (N = 280): relative to a neutral video, it increased empathic concern by d = 0.96 while remaining acceptable regarding distress, disgust, threat, reactance, trust, and comprehensibility (see Section S1.5 of the Supplemental Materials).

Of the 653 participants assigned to the empathy-induction condition, 624 (95.6%) completed the writing task, spending a median of 186 s on the intervention page (the video itself lasted 1 min 17 s); the median participant wrote 22 words.

Immediately afterwards, 622 (95.3%) completed the empathic-concern measure (α = .97) and reported moderate to high empathic concern (M = 4.48, SD = 1.78, on a scale from 1 to 7), with 48.6% at 5 or above.
This level of empathic concern was significantly higher than in the perspective-taking condition (M = 3.96, SD = 1.77), d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.18, 0.41].
Welfare Tradeoff Ratios.
A person's welfare tradeoff ratio for another person is the decision weight they assign to that person's well-being divided by the decision weight they assign to their own well-being.

We measured each participant's welfare tradeoff ratios for four others from different social groups: a transgender individual, an immigrant, a person who is lesbian, gay, or bisexual, and someone from their immediate family.
We measured these four welfare tradeoff ratios using an adapted version of the lambda slider measure developed by Qi et al. (2025).
text.formatted: We measured these four welfare tradeoff ratios using an adapted version of the lambda slider measure developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Qi et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: For each of the four people, participants were asked to imagine they could increase their own well-being and the well-being of that other person.
They then used the lambda slider to select the added amounts of well-being for themselves and the other entity that looked best to them.
The lambda slider is constructed such that the slider position generating the combination that is best according to a participant's social preferences is equal to their welfare tradeoff ratio.
We created three blocks of four incentive-compatible donation decisions each.
Each participant completed the first two blocks in random order: one before the intervention and one after.
We presented the third block in the follow-up survey.
Participants knew that, for each part, we would randomly select two participants and pay out one of their decisions.
In each donation decision, participants decided how to split $100 between themselves and a real charity.
Each trial involved a different charity.
No charity was presented twice to the same participant.

Each block included four types of charities: one helping transgender people (e.g., Trans Lifeline), one helping immigrants (e.g., National Immigration Law Center), one seeking to restrict transgender rights (e.g., Women's Liberation Front), and one aiming to restrict immigration and/or reduce protections for immigrants (e.g., Institute for Sound Public Policy).

We used the amount of money a participant donated to the protransgender and pro-immigration charities as a measure of their outgroup prosociality toward transgender people and immigrants, respectively.
Conversely, we used the amount of money a participant donated to the anti-trans and anti-immigration charities as a measure of their hostility toward transgender people and immigrants, respectively.
We informed participants of each charity's name, primary beneficiaries, programs, impact, and Charity Navigator ratings.
We also provided participants with a link to each charity's website and its Charity Navigator profile.

We drafted the donation-option descriptions with Claude Opus (Anthropic, 2025 (Anthropic, -2026) from publicly available information about each charity and reviewed, verified, and edited them before use.
text.formatted: We drafted the donation-option descriptions with Claude Opus <ref type="bibr">(Anthropic, 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Anthropic, -2026</ref>) from publicly available information about each charity and reviewed, verified, and edited them before use.

text.text: Donation-based measures of effectiveness focus.

We measured how effectively people pursue their prosocial motives by how they split a donation between a highly effective charity and a symbolic or commemorative organization serving the same population.
Each allocation decision was incentive-compatible because it was included in the set of decisions that two randomly selected participants might make.
We created three blocks of three allocation decisions each.

In every block, participants split $100 between i) a highly cost-effective global health charity (Helen Keller International, the Malaria Consortium, or the Against Malaria In addition to these behavioral measures, we administered eight measures of participants' feelings and beliefs about the target groups.
Table 4 summarizes each measure's construct, source, and response format; Section S1.4 of the Supplemental Materials provides the full descriptions.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">4</ref> summarizes each measure's construct, source, and response format; Section S1.4 of the Supplemental Materials provides the full descriptions.

text.text: Reliability.
All multi-item scales' internal-consistency estimates (Cronbach's α) were acceptable to excellent (αs ≥ .79) at both assessments.
We report the Cronbach's α values computed from our dataset in Table S1.3.
text.formatted: We report the Cronbach's α values computed from our dataset in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>.3.

text.text: We followed the preregistered analysis plan (https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf) and conducted additional exploratory analyses, clearly labeled as such.
text.formatted: We followed the preregistered analysis plan (<ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/zp8w7d.pdf</ref>) and conducted additional exploratory analyses, clearly labeled as such.

text.text: In general, our analyses use linear models with covariates measuring preexisting individual differences in the dependent variable, when available, or one or more closely related variables, otherwise.
The linear models also included interaction effects between this measure of pre-existing differences in the construct of interest and the experimental condition.
All covariates were grand-mean centered.
As preregistered, we used one-tailed tests for all directional preregistered hypotheses and did not control for multiple comparisons.

For each model, we additionally report a covariate-adjusted standardized effect size, dadj, computed as the model's condition coefficient divided by the raw standard deviation of the outcome among analyzed participants (Morris & DeShon, 2002).
text.formatted: For each model, we additionally report a covariate-adjusted standardized effect size, dadj, computed as the model's condition coefficient divided by the raw standard deviation of the outcome among analyzed participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Morris & DeShon, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: This retains the metric of Cohen's d while using the more precise covariate-adjusted estimate of the group difference; in models with a Condition × baseline interaction, dadj estimates the effect at the sample-mean baseline.
Analyses of Part 3.
We followed the Part 3 preregistration (https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf), except for the deviations listed in Table S1.7.1 of the Supplemental Materials.
text.formatted: We followed the Part 3 preregistration (<ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/2pz5ei.pdf</ref>), except for the deviations listed in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>.7.1 of the Supplemental Materials.

text.text: The primary contrast compared SMR with neutral reflection.

Outcomes measured at all three post-intervention assessments (donations to charities helping transgender people, welfare tradeoff ratios, and dehumanization) were analyzed with mixed-effects models for repeated measures (R package mmrm; Sabanés Bové et al., 2025) that included condition, assessment, and their interaction; the pre-intervention measure of the outcome (for dehumanization, closely related pre-intervention attitudes) and its interactions with assessment and condition; and gender.
These models used an unstructured covariance matrix and Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom (Kenward & Roger, 1997).
text.formatted: These models used an unstructured covariance matrix and Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Kenward & Roger, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: As preregistered, these models used all available observations of the 1,156 SMR and NR participants in the Part 1 sample, including those who did not complete Part 3 (620 did); this yields unbiased estimates if the missing observations are missing at random given the observed ones.
As in Parts 1 and 2, the donations of participants who failed a part's charity-comprehension check were excluded from that part's observations.

Each prediction was tested with the SMR-NR contrast in Part 3, computed with the R package emmeans (Lenth, 2025), and decay was estimated as the change in this contrast from immediately after the intervention to Part 3.
text.formatted: Each prediction was tested with the SMR-NR contrast in Part 3, computed with the R package emmeans <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lenth, 2025)</ref>, and decay was estimated as the change in this contrast from immediately after the intervention to Part 3.

text.text: Outcomes measured only in Part 3 were analyzed with the linear models described above.
As in Parts 1 and 2, directional predictions were tested one-tailed, and dadj was computed with the standard deviation of the outcome in Part 3.
The two tests of whether the transfer effects persisted were Holm-corrected (Holm, 1979).
text.formatted: The two tests of whether the transfer effects persisted were Holm-corrected <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Holm, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Ascent of Man scale (Kteily et al., 2015) Slider from 0 to 100 rating "how evolved" each group is perceived to be were significantly improved (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Ascent of Man scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kteily et al., 2015)</ref> Slider from 0 to 100 rating "how evolved" each group is perceived to be were significantly improved (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>).

text.text: Below, we report these effects from strongest to weakest.
Behavior Toward the Target Group Donations to charities helping the target group.

Consistent with Prediction 1, the component of people's attitudes toward the target group that SMR improved the most was their behavior toward the outgroup, as demonstrated by an increase in the costly prosocial behavior of donating money to charities helping the outgroup.
As predicted, participants who completed SMR subsequently allocated more money to a charity helping transgender people than participants who reflected on leisure activities.
After adjusting for pre-reflection donations and gender, SMR participants donated $9.93 more (out of $100) than neutral-reflection participants, b = 9.93, t(843) = 6.09, p < .001 (one-tailed).
text.formatted: After adjusting for pre-reflection donations and gender, SMR participants donated $9.93 more (out of $100) than neutral-reflection participants, b = 9.93, t(843) = 6.09, p < .001 (one-tailed).

text.text: Compared to neutral reflection, SMR increased the average raw donation amount from $36.52 (SD = 33.53) to $46.10 (SD = 38.12), dadj = 0.27, 95% CI [0.19, 0.36], and the median donation increased from $30 to $50, which meant splitting the endowment 50/50 (see Figure 4).
text.formatted: Compared to neutral reflection, SMR increased the average raw donation amount from $36.52 (SD = 33.53) to $46.10 (SD = 38.12), dadj = 0.27, 95% CI [0.19, 0.36], and the median donation increased from $30 to $50, which meant splitting the endowment 50/50 (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">4</ref>).

text.text: The effect did not depend on participants' pre-reflection giving (Condition × baseline interaction, p = .921), indicating that SMR raised donations across the full range of baseline generosity toward the target group, rather than only among those already inclined to support them.
Willingness to interact with the target group.
SMR also increased participants' willingness to choose a transgender person as a social partner.

Adjusting for gender as well as transgender-related warmth, donations, and welfare tradeoff ratios at pre-test, participants who completed SMR reported significantly greater willingness to interact with transgender individuals than participants who reflected on leisure activities, b = 0.17, t(1092) = 2.74, p = .003 (onetailed), dadj = 0.11, 95% CI [0.03, 0.18].
The effect did not depend on participants' pre-reflection warmth toward transgender people (Condition × baseline interaction, p = .151).
We next asked whether SMR shifted participants' welfare tradeoff ratios (WTRs) toward transgender people, that is, the weight they placed on a transgender stranger's welfare relative to their own.

Regressing post-reflection WTR on condition while controlling for pre-reflection WTR and gender, participants in the SMR condition placed significantly greater weight on transgender welfare than those in the neutralreflection condition, b = 0.08, t(1056) = 3.21, p < .001 (one-tailed); the raw mean WTR rose from 0.33 following neutral reflection to 0.45 following SMR.
text.formatted: Regressing post-reflection WTR on condition while controlling for pre-reflection WTR and gender, participants in the SMR condition placed significantly greater weight on transgender welfare than those in the neutralreflection condition, b = 0.08, t(1056) = 3.21, p < .001 (one-tailed); the raw mean WTR rose from 0.33 following neutral reflection to 0.45 following SMR.

text.text: The standardized effect was small but reliably positive, dadj = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.19].

This increase was qualified by a significant Condition × baseline-WTR interaction, b = -0.10, t(1056) = -2.38, p = .018: the SMR-induced gain was larger among participants who began with lower welfare weights on transgender people and smaller among those who already placed high weight on their welfare.
SMR reduced the dehumanization of transgender people.
As predicted, SMR significantly reduced blatant dehumanization of transgender people.

Adjusting for gender and baseline attitudes (pre-reflection warmth, donations, and welfare tradeoff ratios), participants who completed SMR dehumanized transgender people significantly less than participants who completed neutral reflection, b = -5.06, t(1091) = -3.57, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.18, 95% CI [-0.28, -0.08].
text.formatted: Adjusting for gender and baseline attitudes (pre-reflection warmth, donations, and welfare tradeoff ratios), participants who completed SMR dehumanized transgender people significantly less than participants who completed neutral reflection, b = -5.06, t(1091) = -3.57, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.18, 95% CI [-0.28, -0.08].

text.text: This effect did not depend on participants' baseline attitudes towards transgender people (Condition × baseline interaction, p = .417).
SMR also increased support for policies protecting or expanding the rights of transgender people.

Adjusting for pre-reflection welfare tradeoff ratios, warmth, and gender, participants in the SMR condition expressed significantly greater support for policies protecting or extending transgender rights than participants in the neutral-reflection condition, b = 0.16, t(1093) = 2.35, p = .010 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.02, 0.18].
The effect did not vary with baseline welfare tradeoff ratios (p = .190).
No effect on the perceived moral standing of transgender people.
Contrary to our prediction, SMR did not move transgender people closer to the center of participants' moral circles.

Controlling for the same baseline covariates, the effect of condition on moral-circle placement was nonsignificant and directionally negative, b = -0.004, t(1052) = -0.36, p = .639 (one-tailed; p = .721, two-tailed), dadj = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.08].
Target Group SMR also improved the affective component of participants' attitudes toward the target group.

Controlling for pre-reflection warmth and gender, participants who completed SMR reported significantly warmer feelings toward transgender people than participants who reflected on leisure activities, b = 4.03, t(1151) = 5.49, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.13, 95% CI [0.08, 0.17].
text.formatted: Controlling for pre-reflection warmth and gender, participants who completed SMR reported significantly warmer feelings toward transgender people than participants who reflected on leisure activities, b = 4.03, t(1151) = 5.49, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.13, 95% CI [0.08, 0.17].

text.text: A significant Condition × baseline-warmth interaction, b = -0.08, t(1151) = -3.49, p < .001, indicated that SMR produced the largest increases in warmth among participants with the least favorable initial feelings toward transgender people.
text.formatted: A significant Condition × baseline-warmth interaction, b = -0.08, t(1151) = -3.49, p < .001, indicated that SMR produced the largest increases in warmth among participants with the least favorable initial feelings toward transgender people.

text.text: How Do the Effects of SMR Compare to Empathy Induction and Perspective-Taking?

We next asked whether the benefits of SMR merely reflect demand characteristics, perspective-taking, or empathy, or whether SMR outperforms established prejudice-reduction interventions that elicit only those processes but not systematic moral reflection.

To this end, we compare the SMR condition against two state-of-the-art prejudice-reduction interventions based on empathy induction (EI) and perspective-taking (PT), using the same covariate-adjusted models with SMR as the reference group and one-tailed tests of the preregistered prediction that SMR would outperform each comparison condition.
Donations to charities helping the target group.

Consistent with Prediction 6, SMR outperformed every comparison condition on motivating people to help the target group at a personal cost, as measured by donations to a charity helping transgender people (see Figure 4).
text.formatted: Consistent with Prediction 6, SMR outperformed every comparison condition on motivating people to help the target group at a personal cost, as measured by donations to a charity helping transgender people (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">4</ref>).

text.text: Adjusting for gender and pre-reflection donations, the SMR group donated $3.49 more than the empathy-induction group, t(1617) = 2.27, p = .012 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.18] and $5.63 more than the perspective-taking group, t(1617) = 3.64, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.16, 95% CI [0.07, 0.24].
text.formatted: Adjusting for gender and pre-reflection donations, the SMR group donated $3.49 more than the empathy-induction group, t(1617) = 2.27, p = .012 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.18] and $5.63 more than the perspective-taking group, t(1617) = 3.64, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.16, 95% CI [0.07, 0.24].

text.text: Because empathy induction and perspective-taking plausibly produce at least as much experimental demand and emotional engagement as SMR, SMR's advantage over these active interventions cannot readily be attributed to demand characteristics or transient emotional arousal.

Moreover, because the empathy-induction and perspective-taking conditions each deliver one of SMR's familiar ingredients on its own, SMR's advantage over both interventions indicates that its benefits are not reducible to the empathy or perspective-taking components it contains.
Therefore, its distinctive element of guiding people to learn lessons from their own past moral decisions may contribute beyond these established components.
Moreover, SMR's significant benefit over neutral reflection shows that its benefit is not merely due to putting people into a more reflective and analytical mindset either.
An exploratory follow-up analysis addressed the further alternative explanation that SMR outperformed the comparison interventions simply because its higher intensity induced more empathic concern.
It did not.

Participants in the SMR condition reported significantly less empathic concern for transgender people than participants in the empathy-induction condition, b = -0.48, SE = 0.11, t(2166) = -4.42, p < .001, and the neutral-reflection group, b = -0.36, SE = 0.11, t(2166) = -3.34, p = .001, while donating more than both.foot_3 SMR thus increased costly helping without increasing the affective response that empathy induction is designed to elicit.
text.formatted: Participants in the SMR condition reported significantly less empathic concern for transgender people than participants in the empathy-induction condition, b = -0.48, SE = 0.11, t(2166) = -4.42, p < .001, and the neutral-reflection group, b = -0.36, SE = 0.11, t(2166) = -3.34, p = .001, while donating more than both.<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> SMR thus increased costly helping without increasing the affective response that empathy induction is designed to elicit.

text.text: Note.

Distributions of donations to charities helping transgender people immediately after the intervention (in $ of the $100 endowment) in the systematic-moral-reflection (SMR), empathyinduction (EI), perspective-taking (PT), and neutral-reflection (NR) conditions.

For each condition, the box plot summarizes the raw donations (horizontal line = median; box = interquartile range; whiskers = 1.5 × the interquartile range), the gray dashes to its left show the individual participants' donations, and the shaded curve to its right shows their smoothed distribution.

The black horizontal line to the right of each distribution marks the covariateadjusted mean donation in that condition (adjusting for participants' pre-intervention donation and gender), and the green error bar around it is the 95% confidence interval of that adjusted mean.
Higher values indicate that more of the $100 was donated to the charity helping the outgroup.
Welfare tradeoff ratios for the target group.

SMR increased participants' decision weights for the target group's welfare more than perspective-taking, b = 0.06, t(2105) = 2.36, p = .009 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.09, 95% CI [0.01, 0.16], while its advantage over empathy induction was marginal, b = 0.04, t(2105) = 1.62, p = .053 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.13].
Willingness to interact with the target group.

SMR increased participants' willingness to choose a transgender person as a social partner relative to perspective-taking, b = 0.14, t(2176) = 2.36, p = .009 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.09, 95% CI [0.02, 0.17], but not relative to empathy induction, b = 0.03, p = .292 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.054, 0.096].
Policy beliefs.

SMR increased support for transgender-protective policies relative to perspective-taking, b = 0.16, t(2178) = 2.38, p = .009 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.02, 0.18], but not relative to empathy induction, b = 0.07, p = .139 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.12].
Beliefs about the moral standing of transgender people.

SMR moved transgender people closer to the center of participants' moral circles relative to perspective-taking, b = 0.02, t(2103) = 2.09, p = .018 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.19], but not relative to empathy induction, b = 0.01, p = .285 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.12].

According to an exploratory analysis, SMR reduced dehumanization of transgender people more than the perspective-taking intervention, b = 3.88, t(2176) = 2.68, p = .007, dadj = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24], but not relative to empathy induction, b = 1.18, t(2176) = 0.83, p = .407, dadj = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.14], although the difference favored SMR numerically.
Warmth toward the target group.
SMR made participants feel warmer toward transgender people than either of the two established interventions.

Thus, relative to SMR, warmth toward transgender people was significantly lower in the perspective-taking condition, b = -2.70, t(2301) = -3.84, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.13, -0.04], and in the empathy induction condition, b = -1.29, t(2301) = -1.86, p = .031 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.00].
text.formatted: Thus, relative to SMR, warmth toward transgender people was significantly lower in the perspective-taking condition, b = -2.70, t(2301) = -3.84, p < .001 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.13, -0.04], and in the empathy induction condition, b = -1.29, t(2301) = -1.86, p = .031 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.00].

text.text: A key question for any prejudice-reduction intervention is whether its benefits are confined to the group featured in the intervention or transfer to other outgroups (Prediction 5).
The SMR materials concerned a decision about transgender people; neither immigrants nor lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) people were mentioned in any part of this intervention.
We therefore tested whether SMR nevertheless improved attitudes toward these untargeted groups relative to neutral reflection (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: We therefore tested whether SMR nevertheless improved attitudes toward these untargeted groups relative to neutral reflection (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>).

text.text: Finally, we also tested how the transgenderfocussed version of the SMR intervention affected people's attitudes toward charities seeking to protect cisgender women from transgender women.

The effect of systematic moral reflection on a decision about helping transgender people transferred to improvements in all three aspects of participants' attitudes toward immigrants: affect, cognitions, and behavior (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: The effect of systematic moral reflection on a decision about helping transgender people transferred to improvements in all three aspects of participants' attitudes toward immigrants: affect, cognitions, and behavior (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>).

text.text: The analyses reported in this section tested this hypothesis with linear models controlling for each DV's level prior to the intervention and participants' immigrant identity.
Donations to pro-immigrant charities.

Following SMR participants donated significantly more money to charities helping immigrants and refugees (M = $49.99, SD = $35.59) than after NR (M = $43.89, SD = $33.72), b = 3.44, t(840) = 2.22, p = .013 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.19].
This effect was strongest for participants who had donated less to pro-immigrant charities prior to the intervention, b = -0.11, t(840) = -2.25, p = .025.
Following SMR, participants assigned more weigh to immigrants' welfare (M = 0.57) than following NR (M = 0.46), b = 0.06, t(1055) = 2.94, p = .002 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.11, 95% CI [0.04, 0.18].
Willingness to partner with immigrants.

Following SMR, participants reported a greater willingness to form social relationships with immigrants (M = 5.93) than after NR (M = 5.78), b = 0.15, t(1088) = 2.53, p = .006 (one-tailed), dadj = 0.12, 95% CI [0.03, 0.21].
According to an exploratory analysis paralleling the finding for transgender people, SMR significantly reduced the blatant dehumanization of immigrants (M = 9.16, SD = 17.26, vs.
M = 11.98, SD = 19.77, after neutral reflection), b = -2.80, t(1100) = -2.70, p = .007 (two-tailed), dadj = -0.15, 95% CI [-0.26, -0.04], compared to neutral reflection.
Dehumanization of the ingroup ("real Americans") was unaffected (see Section S2.4).
As with the target group, SMR did not affect where participants placed immigrants in their moral circle (M = 0.56, SD = 0.20, vs.
M = 0.56, SD = 0.22, after neutral reflection), b = -0.01, t(1048) = -0.46, p = .677 (one-tailed), dadj = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.09], compared to NR.

A further exploratory analysis found that SMR increased participants' warmth toward immigrants (M = 72.93), b = 2.20, t(1139) = 3.89, p < .001 (twotailed), dadj = 0.09, 95% CI [0.05, 0.14], compared to NR (M = 71.80).
text.formatted: A further exploratory analysis found that SMR increased participants' warmth toward immigrants (M = 72.93), b = 2.20, t(1139) = 3.89, p < .001 (twotailed), dadj = 0.09, 95% CI [0.05, 0.14], compared to NR (M = 71.80).

text.text: As for warmth toward transgender people, this effect was strongest for participants with initially colder feelings toward immigrants, b = -0.07, p = .007.
As predicted, the effect of SMR also transferred to people's regard for people identifying as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB).
Compared to NR, SMR significantly increased the weight participants placed on the welfare of an LGB stranger, b = 0.09, t(1077) = 3.79, p < .001 (onetailed), dadj = 0.13, 95% CI [0.07, 0.20].
text.formatted: Compared to NR, SMR significantly increased the weight participants placed on the welfare of an LGB stranger, b = 0.09, t(1077) = 3.79, p < .001 (onetailed), dadj = 0.13, 95% CI [0.07, 0.20].

text.text: This effect was larger for participants for whom this moral weight was lower prior to the intervention (Condition × baseline interaction, b = -0.09, p = .016).
